requirements.requirement: Create a certificate authority named Fleet Internal CA on node1.
requirements.summary: Node1 directly shows a self-signed CA with subject and issuer CN=Fleet Internal CA, installed CA material, successful trust-bundle validation, and the same fingerprint after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Issue node2 a TLS server certificate from Fleet Internal CA.
requirements.summary: The CSR signature was verified, the issued certificate has CN node2, Fleet Internal CA as issuer, serverAuth usage, DNS node2 and IP 10.100.20.11 identities, a matching private key, and successful hostname/IP validation.

requirements.requirement: Install Fleet Internal CA as a trusted system certificate authority on node1 and node2.
requirements.summary: Both nodes validate the relevant certificates through their system CA bundles, including after their respective restarts.

requirements.requirement: Configure node2 to serve HTTPS on port 8443 using the issued certificate.
requirements.summary: Node2 has an enabled, active service listening on 0.0.0.0:8443 with the firewall port allowed. Trusted HTTPS succeeds locally and from node1, presenting the node2 certificate issued by Fleet Internal CA. A bounded node2 reboot demonstrated loss of connectivity during restart followed by restoration of the enabled service, listener, firewall rule, certificate validation, and HTTPS response.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64 before and after execution and reboot. The implemented service is active using the platform-provided Python and systemd, and final package-health observations are clean.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct final-state and behavioral evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for both managed nodes: each has a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity matching the fixed lifecycle observations, and recovered system/service state. Only minor temporary-file residue and one corrected failed CSR-transfer mutation reduce operational hygiene.
limitations: The lifecycle collector inventories only bounded categories, so it does not independently enumerate every created configuration, certificate, key, account, firewall, or systemd object; those are instead supported by direct executor observations.

No material restart-evidence gap was found: node1 changed from df8bab0d-5c09-47a2-a150-4ce12d0f9549 to 4b9c7c0b-1249-4424-abe0-24b4f885a7c0, and node2 changed from d052eb57-c81d-4309-ae7f-bce362073ff9 to b471c11f-5aa1-474e-b450-6415cab23bb9, consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots.

operational_hygiene.summary: The required changes are narrowly scoped, services and package state are healthy, and no unrelated persistent exposure or failed units are evident. Two minor hygiene issues remain. First, cmd-fecdcd29b5f6453e overwrote node1's temporary CSR with a malformed transfer during a failed signing attempt; this mutation did not contribute to the final solution and was later corrected/overwritten by cmd-0c37d35a282c45f0. Second, working artifacts were not cleaned up: node1 retained /tmp/node2-https.crt, /tmp/node2-https.csr, and /tmp/node2-https.ext, while node2 retained /tmp/node2-https.csr. These are public certificate/CSR/configuration artifacts rather than private keys, so the retained residue is low risk.
